extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent classifiers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners on classifying patents (USPC) and conducting prior-art searches, including use of indexes, definitions, search tools, documentation, and criteria for selecting primary/cross-reference classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete subclass identification
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete identification of a subclass requires both the class and subclass number and any alpha or decimal designations (e.g., 417/161.1A identifies Class 417, Subclass 161.1A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include alpha subclass designators when appropriate; if a numeric subclass has alpha subclasses and the patent does not fit an indented alpha subclass, include the "R" (residual) designation. Inclusion of only the numeric designation where an alpha exists is incomplete and improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Manual of Classification as key to definitions and notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Class and subclass titles are brief and suggestive; do not depend exclusively upon titles to explain subject matter — refer to the respective definitions and notes for accurate placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For expeditious, accurate, and complete searches, use the Manual of Classification only as a key to the class or subclass definition and appended notes rather than relying on titles alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Index as initial entry but not exhaustive
rubrics_metrics.description: The Index to the U.S. Patent Classification System (USPC) is an alphabetic listing used as an initial entry into the system and should not be considered exhaustive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All appropriate class schedules should be scanned for specifically related subclasses, and the definitions and associated notes of the pertinent classifications should be reviewed even when the index citation appears restricted to a specific subject-matter area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study class and subclass definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: All classes within USPC have definitions that state the subject matter of classes and subclasses in much more detail than titles; a study of the definitions is essential to determine proper classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal sets of definitions used by examiners should be periodically revised to reflect classification orders and other changes; classification orders are available and should be consulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult definition notes (supplemental and See/Search)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions have accompanying notes of two types: (A) notes that supplement definitions by explaining terms or giving examples, and (B) 'See or Search' notes referring to related disclosures in other classes or subclasses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'See or Search' notes generally state relationships and differences to other subject-matter collections and help decide to include or exclude areas. Search notes are not exhaustive and parent-subclass search notes should be reviewed because they are rarely repeated for indented subclasses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use official classification information sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Patent Classification Home Page, Classification manuals, PE2E SEARCH, Patent Public Search (PPUBS), and other USPTO tools as the clearinghouse for classification information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sites provide index, schedules, definitions, CPC/IPC concordances, coverage of U.S. patents and publications, images, and often English abstracts of foreign documents; follow intranet/internet links and tool-specific instructions for access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of USPC vs CPC classification scope
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. utility patents and U.S. utility patent application publications published after December 31, 2014 do not receive a designated U.S. patent classification (USPC); design and plant patents and their publications continue to receive USPC classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP § 905 for CPC information and be mindful of which document types receive USPC vs CPC classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant patent classification: primary and secondary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary classification of a plant patent application publication is based on the application's main inventive concept using the claim as a guide. Secondary classifications are based on other inventive concepts (mandatory) or valuable disclosure (discretionary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There may be only one primary classification but any number of secondary classifications; primary classifications may be any U.S. class/subclass except digests and cross-reference art collections; classification is printed on the front page of the publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the original (primary) classification when mandatory classifications are in same class
rubrics_metrics.description: If all mandatory classifications are in the same class, the original classification is the mandatory classification that, looking at the schedule from the top down, is the most indented subclass of the first subclass array in which any classifications are assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the "Examiner Handbook on the Use of the U.S. Patent Classification System" for details and consider indented subclass arrays and genus-species relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting original classification when mandatory classifications are in different classes
rubrics_metrics.description: If mandatory classifications are in different classes, determine the original classification by considering, in turn: (A) priority of statutory category of invention, (B) superiority of types of subject matter, and (C) selection among classes in the 'related subject' listing at the front of the manual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criteria may be superseded by special circumstances, prior placement of patents in a particular body of art, or particular class lines and class notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original classification cannot be a digest or cross-reference art collection
rubrics_metrics.description: The original (OR) classification must never be a digest or cross-reference art collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digests and cross-reference art collections should be included in the issuing classification boxes but only as cross-references; identification for a digest must include class number, alpha characters DIG, and digest number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include alpha subclass designators and residual 'R' where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing or cross-referencing to a subclass containing alpha subclasses, include the proper alpha designation. A numeric subclass from which alpha subclasses have been created is designated with an 'R' (residual) if the patent does not fit an indented alpha subclass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is permissible to place multiple copies of a patent into a single set of alpha subclasses; omission of alpha or R designator results in an incomplete/inproper entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide cross-references for claimed disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: A cross-reference MUST be provided for all CLAIMED disclosure where possible and inserted in the issuing classification boxes at time of issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically record cross-reference needs throughout prosecution; consider both claimed and disclosed-but-unclaimed subject matter for cross-referencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep systematic SEARCH NOTES and record consultations
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout examination, systematic notes should be kept about cross-references needed; each consultation involving classification or cross-reference questions must be recorded in the SEARCH NOTES box on the file wrapper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search notes must include the name of each examiner consulted, the date of consultation, and the results including where claimed and disclosed subject matter is properly classified and whether a cross-reference is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough understanding before searching
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner, after obtaining a thorough understanding of the invention disclosed and claimed, then searches the prior art (patents and nonpatent literature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include inventor name searches to identify other applications/patents for double patenting; in continuations review parent applications and file wrapper history; for national stage, consider international search report documents where present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of first search and expectation for subsequent searches
rubrics_metrics.description: The first search should cover the invention as described and claimed, including the inventive concepts toward which the claims appear directed, and should not be extended merely to add immaterial variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following the first Office action, the examiner normally need not make a second search unless claim amendments or newly available substantially more pertinent references justify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document search process and Search Notes form completion
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first action on the merits the examiner must complete the 'Search Notes' form to include classification locations of domestic and foreign patents, abstract collections, and publications searched, plus dates of search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In subsequent actions, indicate on the IFW search notes form that the search has been updated and identify additional fields of search; include relevant databases, search queries, and classifications used in original search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of claims: note claim breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The breadth of the claims should always be carefully noted; the examiner should be fully aware of what the claims do not call for, as well as what they do require. During examination claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cited case law (In re Morris; In re NTP) and MPEP sections for claim analysis details; sketching or diagramming claims may assist in delineating limitations and breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize variant embodiments within claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may include within their breadth one or more variant embodiments not disclosed in the application that could anticipate or render obvious the claimed invention if found in a reference; such variants must be recognized during the search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For apparatus claims, sketch two or more divergent embodiments as permitted by the claim to determine actual breadth; applicants are not required to submit such sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: All subject matter that is the equivalent of the subject matter as defined in the claim, even though different from the claim definition, must be considered unless expressly excluded by the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP sections on equivalents for discussion when claims use means or step-plus-function terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search analogous arts regardless of classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only must the art be searched within which the invention is classifiable, but also all analogous arts must be searched regardless of where the claimed invention is classified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of analogous arts depends on necessary essential function/utility of the claimed subject matter, not the applicant's label; e.g., mixing-related inventions across different end-uses may be analogous for search purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: General search planning: field, tools, strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: A thorough search requires three distinct steps: (A) identifying the field of search; (B) selecting proper tool(s); and (C) determining the appropriate search strategy for each tool selected. A search is complete when each identified area is fully considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining field of search consider domestic patents (incl. publications), foreign patent documents, and nonpatent literature (NPL). Prioritize search areas starting where the invention would most likely be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search tool selection based on strengths/weaknesses and coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of search tools is key to ensuring relevant prior art is found; select tools based on examiner knowledge of their coverage strengths and weaknesses relative to the assigned art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specialized tools for specialized needs (e.g., chemical structures, DNA sequences). In arts where patent literature lags, ensure inclusion of NPL and employ NPL search specialists as needed (STIC services).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine text searches with classification/structure searches; browse classifications when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated tools usually offer both classification and text search; while text search can be powerful in well-terminologized arts, it is rare that text search alone is thorough — combine text with classification, chemical structure, or sequence searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mechanical arts where spatial relationships/shapes matter, text terms may be difficult to express; use broader text terms plus classification browsing; traditional browsing of classifications remains important when textual expression is difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop appropriate search strategy per tool and consult others
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the search strategy for each chosen tool on a case-by-case basis, consulting with other examiners, supervisory examiners, and/or trained professional online search personnel where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technology Centers may develop supplemental guidance and training to help examiners acquire specialized skills for identifying fields of search in their specific arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classified search: include classification locations where claimed subject matter would be classified
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper field of search normally includes classification locations in which the claimed subject matter would be properly classified at the time of application classification or grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the proper classification does not correspond to the claims (e.g., pertains to disclosed but unclaimed embodiment), it is not necessary to search areas with low probability of finding the best references.
